191.quote_or_event: “O Nanak, speaking insipid words, the body and mind become insipid. He is called the most insipid of the insipid; the most insipid of the insipid is his reputation.”
191.explanation: In a salok of Asa ki Vaar, Guru Nanak warns that fikaa (tasteless, graceless) speech hollows out the speaker and leaves him with a reputation as hollow as his words.
191.tie_back: The Kural says the man who keeps pouring out useless talk ends up scorned by everyone; Guru Nanak likewise says the insipid talker becomes known to all by that insipidness.
191.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 473, Raag Aasaa (Asa ki Vaar, salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
191._accuracy_note: Strong fit: both tie empty speech to a ruined public standing; the salok does not mention the listeners growing weary, which is the Kural's specific image.

192.quote_or_event: “To speak too much and babble is useless.”
192.explanation: In a hymn in Raag Dhanaasree, Guru Nanak dismisses endless talk and babbling as worthless.
192.tie_back: The Kural ranks pointless talk before many people as worse than wronging one's friends; Guru Nanak shares the low estimate of babble, though he makes no such comparison.
192.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 661, Raag Dhanaasree, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
192._accuracy_note: Next-best only: the line condemns babbling but has nothing of the Kural's startling ranking of idle public talk below unkindness to friends.

193.quote_or_event: “Whatever is in the mind, comes forth; spoken words by themselves are just wind.”
193.explanation: In a salok preserved in Asa ki Vaar, Guru Angad teaches that what a person truly is inside will show itself, while words on their own are only air.
193.tie_back: The Kural says that long talk about worthless things itself announces the speaker's lack of goodness; Guru Angad likewise holds that the inner self comes out and that mere words are empty wind.
193.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 474, Raag Aasaa (Asa ki Vaar, salok), Guru Angad (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
193._accuracy_note: Strong thematic fit on speech exposing the inner person and words as mere wind; the salok is about the heart showing through generally, not specifically through trivial talk.

194.quote_or_event: “By mere talk, people do not earn passage to Heaven. Salvation comes only from the practice of Truth.”
194.explanation: In a salok of Vaar Maajh, Guru Nanak insists that talking gets no one to the goal; only truth lived in action does.
194.tie_back: The Kural says useless, graceless words cut a person off from virtue and goodness; Guru Nanak likewise separates mere talk from the lived truth that alone carries a person forward.
194.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 141, Raag Maajh (Vaar Maajh, salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
194._accuracy_note: Next-best: the verse contrasts talk with practice rather than saying empty talk actively removes one from goodness, and it is addressed to religious hypocrisy, not idle chatter.

195.quote_or_event: “The insipid person is discarded in the Court of the Lord, and the insipid one's face is spat upon.”
195.explanation: Continuing the same salok of Asa ki Vaar, Guru Nanak says the person given to fikaa speech is cast out of the divine Court and disgraced.
195.tie_back: The Kural warns that even people of fine character lose their excellence and honour when they speak empty words; Guru Nanak likewise says such speech costs a person all honour, before God as well as people.
195.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 473, Raag Aasaa (Asa ki Vaar, salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
195._accuracy_note: Reasonable but partial: the loss of honour matches, but the salok does not single out good people who lapse, and it is the same salok used for Kural 191.

196.quote_or_event: “O Nanak, those people are really donkeys; they have no virtue or merit, but still, they are very proud.”
196.explanation: In a salok, Guru Nanak refuses the dignity of the name human to people who show off with no virtue behind it, calling them donkeys.
196.tie_back: The Kural will not call the man who delights in displaying empty words a real man, but the chaff among human beings; Guru Nanak likewise demotes the hollow show-off below the human.
196.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1411, Salok Vaaraan Thay Vadheek, Salok 15, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
196._accuracy_note: Reasonable fit: both deny full humanity to the hollow display-maker with a stark image; Guru Nanak's target is pride without merit rather than empty speech specifically.

197.quote_or_event: “Nanak speaks the Word of Truth; he proclaims the Truth at this, the right time.”
197.explanation: In a hymn in Raag Tilang, sung during Babur's invasion, Guru Nanak openly voiced painful and unwelcome truths about the violence he saw, and closes by saying he speaks the truth because the hour requires it.
197.tie_back: The Kural allows the worthy to say what is not pleasing, but never what is useless; Guru Nanak's hymn is a model of speech that is hard to hear yet full of purpose.
197.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 723, Raag Tilang, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
197._accuracy_note: Reasonable but partial: the hymn exemplifies hard but meaningful truth-telling; it does not itself state the Kural's ranking of the unpleasant above the useless.

198.quote_or_event: “O Nanak, only one thing is of any account: everything else is useless babbling and idle talk in ego.”
198.explanation: In a salok of Asa ki Vaar, Guru Nanak says that only the praise and remembrance of the One counts, and all other talk is the idle babble of haumai (ego).
198.tie_back: The Kural says the wise, who seek rare and great benefit, never speak words lacking great benefit; Guru Nanak likewise holds that only words of the highest worth count and the rest is ego's chatter.
198.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 467, Raag Aasaa (Asa ki Vaar, salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
198._accuracy_note: Strong thematic fit on refusing all but the most valuable speech; for Guru Nanak the one thing of account is devotion to God, a narrower and more spiritual standard than the Kural's great benefit.

199.quote_or_event: “Without the Name, all other praise and speech is insipid and tasteless.”
199.explanation: In Raag Gauree, Guru Ram Das teaches that to one who knows the Naam, every other kind of talk loses its taste.
199.tie_back: The Kural says those whose vision is free of delusion will not speak meaningless words even by a slip; Guru Ram Das likewise says the awakened find all speech without the Name empty.
199.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 301, Raag Gauree, Guru Ram Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
199._accuracy_note: Reasonable but partial: both link clear spiritual sight to the end of empty speech, but the verse does not address slips of forgetfulness and centres on the Name rather than on freedom from delusion.

200.quote_or_event: “Those words are acceptable, which, when spoken, bring honor. Harsh words bring only grief. Listen, O foolish and ignorant mind!”
200.explanation: In a hymn in Sri Raag, Guru Nanak sets two kinds of speech side by side: words that bring honour are approved, while fikaa words bring only ruin and grief.
200.tie_back: The Kural closes the chapter by pairing a command to speak only useful words with a ban on useless ones; Guru Nanak builds the same two-sided rule, approving one kind of speech and rejecting the other.
200.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 15, Sri Raag, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
200._accuracy_note: Strong fit in structure and point; Khalsa renders fikaa here as harsh, while the word also means insipid, so the match to useless speech depends partly on that wider sense.
